situation:
You are the customer communications manager and the internal communications manager at COPPERLOOP RECYCLING, a two-year-old electronics recycler that collects used devices, wipes their data, and issues certificates of destruction to households and companies. The co-founder and CEO (judge) has called you in to help settle how the company should decide, and then explain, a change to its walk-in intake policy before word of it reaches customers or staff.

COPPERLOOP built its first two years on two anchor relationships. A regional school district's recycling grant pays for the company's data-destruction equipment on the condition that any household in the district may drop off personal devices for free, certified destruction. A national office-supply retailer separately pays COPPERLOOP a per-device fee to process trade-in laptops and phones from its stores, under a contract that guarantees certified destruction within five business days and carries a penalty for late batches. The retailer's payments cover most of COPPERLOOP's payroll.

Both programs run through the same certified-destruction line, and the district's free program has outgrown its original volume. Word of mouth has brought more households to the drop-off counter each week than the grant ever anticipated, and processing their devices ahead of the retailer's trade-in batches has pushed two recent shipments past the five-day deadline. A third late batch would trigger the retailer's penalty clause at a time when COPPERLOOP's first round of seed funding is nearly spent and has no cushion left to absorb it.

One option on the table is a household cap: keep the district program free up to a set number of devices per family each month, and charge a modest handling fee beyond that limit, so certified-destruction capacity goes to the retailer's batches first. Nothing in the grant agreement or the retailer contract forbids this, but many of the households who have used the free program for two years, some referred by the district itself, are likely to see any fee as the company going back on a promise it made them.

The CEO (judge) wants you to decide whether COPPERLOOP should adopt the cap and fee, hold the program fully free and risk the retailer's penalty, or find another way to protect both relationships, and to recommend how the decision should be communicated to the households affected, to the district, and to COPPERLOOP's own staff who field these questions at the counter.

The CEO (judge) will greet you at the start of the meeting and ask you to walk through your recommendation and the reasoning behind it. Come prepared to explain how you would carry the decision to the counter, to the district, and to the rest of the staff. After your presentation and the questions that follow, the CEO (judge) will thank you for your time and bring the meeting to a close.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the co-founder and CEO (judge) of COPPERLOOP RECYCLING. Business background is the same as the situation above. You want the participants to decide whether COPPERLOOP should adopt the household cap and fee, hold the walk-in program fully free and risk the retailer's penalty, or find another way to protect both relationships, and to recommend how that decision should be communicated to the households affected, to the district, and to your own staff.

You will greet the participants and ask them to share their ideas. After the presentation and the questions below, you will thank the participants. You are not to make any comments after the event is over except to thank the participants.
judgeQuestions: What would you say to a household that has used the free drop-off for two years if it is turned away under the new cap?
What would you tell the retailer's account manager if a certified-destruction batch runs late again next month?
